claims.text: Transition-metal catalyst performance is primarily controlled by the strength of metal–support interactions.
Metal–support interactions modulate the d-band center of supported metal nanoparticles.
Enhancing electronic coupling between a support and a metal causes a downward shift of the metal d-band center.
A downward d-band-center shift changes the adsorption energies of key reaction intermediates.
Changing intermediate adsorption through support-induced electronic coupling can improve catalytic durability, selectivity, and/or activity.
The proposed controlled comparison uses nanoparticles held constant in particle size, dispersion, and oxidation state while changing the support.
The engineered supports systematically vary metal–support interaction strength.
Controlling the feed, reaction conditions, particle properties, and poisoning effects ensures that only metal–support interactions vary.
A support-induced d-band-center shift is the structural/electronic mediator between support choice and catalytic behavior.
Electronic modulation of adsorption optimizes the balance between reactant activation and product desorption.
Avoiding overly strong intermediate binding can prevent catalyst deactivation and unwanted side reactions.
Supports with stronger electronic coupling will produce a measurable downward d-band-center shift relative to the baseline.
Support-induced d-band shifts will modify reaction kinetics relative to the baseline.
Turnover frequency may decrease if intermediates bind too strongly.
Selectivity or durability may improve when intermediate adsorption is optimized.
The hypothesis applies to reactions whose behavior is sensitive to intermediate binding energies under moderate temperature and pressure.
XPS or UPS can be used to characterize the proposed d-band-center shifts.
A lack of systematic correlation between d-band-center shift and activity, selectivity, or durability would falsify the hypothesis.
